title: Ideas That Changed Everything
subtitle: From the first wheel to the World Wide Web
subject: Inventions

p: Humans have been making stone tools for about 3.3 million years. The wheel is only about 5,500 years old. For more than 99 percent of human history, nobody had one. Then somebody had an idea, and the world was never the same. That is what an invention is: an idea that makes a thing possible that was impossible the day before.

Almost no invention appears from nowhere. The wheel needed the axle. The printing press needed paper. The web needed computers, and computers needed electricity. Each idea stands on the ideas before it, like a tower of blocks. This book climbs that tower, one block at a time, from a wooden cart to the screen you may be reading on.
pages.cap: Six ideas, 5,500 years apart at one end and only decades apart at the other.
pages.fact: Did you know? More inventions were patented in the last 30 years than in all the centuries before.

pages.h: The wheel: roll, do not drag
p: The first wheels did not go on carts. About 5,500 years ago in Mesopotamia, now Iraq, potters spun clay on a flat wheel to make pots. Later someone turned a wheel on its side, pushed a rod through the middle and attached it to a box. The cart was born.

Why was it such a big deal? When you drag a heavy load, the whole bottom scrapes along the ground. A wheel touches the ground at one point and rolls over it. Pushing a loaded cart takes about one tenth of the effort of dragging the same load. One person with a cart could move what used to take ten. The hard part was not the wheel. It was the axle, which had to be smooth, round and strong.
pages.cap: A wheel touches the ground at only one spot, so there is far less rubbing than dragging.
pages.fact: Did you know? People in the Americas had wheels more than a thousand years ago, but only on toys. They had no horses or oxen to pull carts.

p: Writing was not invented for stories. It was invented for counting. About 5,200 years ago in the city of Uruk, in Mesopotamia, temple keepers pressed marks into wet clay to record how much barley and how many sheep had come in. The oldest name we know belongs to one of them. Kushim signed a receipt for barley about 5,000 years ago.

Why does writing matter so much? Before it, everything a person knew died with them, or survived only as long as someone remembered. With writing, an idea could outlive its thinker and travel across the world. The first writing used more than 600 picture signs and took years to learn. Alphabets, with about 26 letters, came 1,500 years later and meant almost anyone could learn to read.
pages.cap: Egyptians carved picture-writing called hieroglyphs on their monuments at about the same time Mesopotamians pressed marks into clay.

pages.h: For most of history, almost nobody could read
p: In the year 1500, fewer than 1 in 5 people in Europe could read. Today, nearly 9 in 10 people on Earth can.

pages.q: What was writing first used for?
opts: Counting goods like barley and sheep
pages.why: The oldest writing we have found is lists and receipts. Keeping track of grain and animals was so useful that people worked out a way to record it in clay.

p: In China, around the year 105, a court official named Cai Lun showed how to make paper from mashed bark, rags and fishing nets. By 1040 a Chinese printer called Bi Sheng was pressing pages using clay blocks with one character each, which could be rearranged. Europe had nothing like it for another 400 years.

Around 1450, a German metalworker named Johannes Gutenberg built a press with metal letters, oily ink and a screw mechanism copied from wine presses. Before him, a monk might take a year to copy one Bible by hand. Gutenberg's press could print about 3,000 pages a day. By 1500, Europe had around 20 million printed books. Fifty years earlier it had almost none.
pages.cap: A printing press used a screw and a lever, like a wine press, to stamp inked metal letters onto paper.
pages.fact: Did you know? Gutenberg printed about 180 copies of his Bible. Around 49 still exist, and each is worth millions of dollars.

pages.h: Why cheap books changed the world
p: When books were copied by hand, a single one cost as much as a farm. Only kings, monks and rich merchants owned them. Printing made a book cost about as much as a good meal. Suddenly a farmer's son could own one. Schools opened. Within 150 years, Europe had printed about 200 million books.

Printing did something else. It let scientists compare notes. When Galileo pointed a telescope at the Moon in 1609, he printed his drawings in a small book the next year. All 550 copies sold out, and astronomers across Europe could check his work. Ideas began to spread faster than anyone could stop them. Maps, recipes, laws and news all followed.
pages.cap: Galileo's little printed book of Moon drawings sold out in weeks and let others check what he saw.

p: Make a stamp and discover the printer's biggest headache.
steps: Ask an adult to cut a potato in half. Draw a big letter on the flat side, then ask them to carve away everything around it so the letter stands up.
Press the letter onto a sponge soaked in paint, then stamp it on paper.
Look closely. Your letter is backwards. Printers had to carve every letter in mirror image.
Carve a second potato with the letter drawn backwards. Now it prints the right way round.
pages.cap: A stamp prints its mirror image, so printers had to think backwards.

pages.h: Steam: the power of boiling water
p: When water boils and turns into steam, it swells to about 1,700 times its size. Trap that steam in a cylinder and it pushes like a giant. In 1712 an English ironmonger named Thomas Newcomen built the first useful steam engine. It pumped water out of flooded coal mines, a job that had taken teams of horses walking in circles all day.

In 1769 a Scottish instrument maker, James Watt, found a way to make the engine use a quarter of the coal. Now it was cheap enough to power anything. Watt measured his engines in horses. One could do the work of 20 horses without eating, sleeping or getting tired. Factories no longer had to sit beside rivers. The age of machines had begun.
pages.cap: Boiling water into steam takes up about 1,700 times more room, and that push can drive a piston.
pages.fact: Did you know? We still measure engines in horsepower. One horsepower is about 746 watts, roughly the power of a small hair dryer.

p: In 1804 a Cornish engineer named Richard Trevithick put a steam engine on wheels and hauled 10 tonnes of iron along a track in Wales. In 1829 George Stephenson's locomotive, the Rocket, won a race in England by reaching 48 kilometres per hour. The next year the first passenger railway opened between Liverpool and Manchester.

Why did this matter? For all of history, a traveller on land covered about 50 kilometres a day by horse and cart. A train could cover 500. Fresh fish reached inland cities. Mail arrived in a day instead of a week. In 1885 a railway joined Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. A trip that had taken months on foot took five days by train.
pages.cap: A steam locomotive burned coal to boil water, and the steam pushed pistons that turned the wheels.
pages.fact: Did you know? Early passengers were warned that speeds over 50 kilometres per hour might stop them breathing. It did not happen.

pages.q: What actually pushes the piston in a steam engine?
opts: Steam that swells to 1,700 times the size of the water
pages.why: The coal only heats the water. When the water boils into steam it expands enormously, and that expanding steam shoves the piston along the cylinder.

pages.h: Until 1830, nothing on land carried a person faster than a horse
p: Then came the train. Within 20 years, people were travelling at 100 kilometres per hour, and the world began to shrink.

For thousands of years, when the Sun went down, people lit a flame: a fire, a candle, an oil lamp, a gas lamp. Flames flicker, smoke and burn houses down. In 1879 two inventors working separately, Joseph Swan in England and Thomas Edison in the United States, made a glass bulb glow with electricity.

The trick was the filament, the thin thread inside that gets white hot. Edison's team tested more than 1,000 materials. Cotton thread lasted 13 hours. Then they tried a strip of bamboo, which glowed for 1,200 hours. The bulb worked because the air was pumped out of the glass. With no oxygen, the filament could not burn up. Night was no longer the end of the day.
pages.cap: A thin filament glows white hot inside a glass bulb with the air pumped out, so it cannot burn.
pages.fact: Did you know? Modern LED bulbs use about 85 percent less electricity than Edison's design and last 25 times longer.

p: A bulb is useless without power. In 1882 Edison opened the first electric power station in New York City. It served 82 customers and about 400 lamps. Within 20 years, cities everywhere were stringing wires along their streets. The electric grid may be the biggest machine humans have ever built, with millions of kilometres of wire.

Here is how much has changed. In the year 1800, an hour of candlelight cost about 6 hours of work. Today an hour of light from an LED costs less than one second of work. Electricity brought more than light. It brought refrigerators, washing machines, radios and, in time, computers. Everything in this book after this page runs on it.
pages.cap: A battery or power station pushes electricity along wires, through a switch, and into the bulb.
pages.fact: Did you know? About 60 percent of Canada's electricity comes from falling water in hydroelectric dams.

pages.h: The telephone: a voice through a wire
p: On 10 March 1876, in Boston, a Scottish-born teacher of deaf children named Alexander Graham Bell spoke into a device and his assistant in the next room heard him through a wire. Other inventors, including Elisha Gray and Antonio Meucci, were close to the same idea, and people still argue about who was really first.

How does a telephone work? Your voice is a vibration in the air. It shakes a thin metal disc. The disc wobbles a magnet near a coil of wire, which turns the wobble into an electric current. At the other end, the current wobbles another disc, which shakes the air again. Your voice has been copied in electricity and rebuilt. By 1915 a call could cross North America. By 1927 it could cross the Atlantic.
pages.cap: Sound shakes a disc, the disc makes electricity, and the electricity shakes a disc at the other end.

p: For a hundred years a telephone was tied to a wall. On 3 April 1973 an engineer named Martin Cooper stood on a New York sidewalk and made the first call from a handheld mobile phone. It weighed 1.1 kilograms, about as much as a bag of sugar, gave 30 minutes of talking and took 10 hours to charge.

A phone today weighs about 200 grams. It is a telephone, a camera, a map, a library and a computer in one, and it talks to towers using radio waves instead of wires. More than 4 billion people now carry one. Bell made one connection between two rooms. Your phone can connect you to anyone on Earth in a few seconds.
pages.cap: The first mobile phone weighed more than five modern phones put together.
pages.fact: Did you know? The first mobile phone call was made to a rival engineer at another company, to let him know he had lost the race.

pages.q: In what year did Alexander Graham Bell make the first telephone call?
pages.why: Bell's first call was on 10 March 1876 in Boston. Mobile phones did not arrive until almost a century later, in 1973.

p: The first passengers to fly were a sheep, a duck and a rooster. In 1783 the Montgolfier brothers in France sent them up in a hot-air balloon, and they came down safely. But a balloon only drifts where the wind blows. Real flying needed wings.

Why does a wing lift? It is tilted and curved so that it shoves air downward as it moves forward. Push air down, and the air pushes the wing up. On 17 December 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright, two bicycle makers from Ohio, flew a wooden aircraft with a small engine for 12 seconds and 37 metres. That first flight was shorter than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet. By the end of the day they had flown 260 metres.
pages.cap: A wing pushes air down, and the air pushes the wing up. That upward push is called lift.
pages.fact: Did you know? Only five people watched the Wright brothers' first flight. Most newspapers did not believe it had happened.

p: In 1919 two British pilots crossed the Atlantic nonstop in 16 hours, crash-landing in an Irish bog. In 1927 Charles Lindbergh flew alone from New York to Paris. By the 1950s jet airliners carried hundreds of people at a time. Today about 100,000 flights take off every day.

A jet cruises at about 900 kilometres per hour, 11 kilometres up where the thin air causes less drag. In 1900 a steamship from Montreal to Europe took about a week. A jet does it in 7 hours. Flight changed what distance means. Fresh fruit crosses oceans overnight. A grandparent on the other side of the world is a day away, not a lifetime.
pages.cap: A sailing ship needed about six weeks to cross the Atlantic. A jet needs about seven hours.

pages.h: Try it: lift a paper wing
p: Feel the push that keeps a 400 tonne airplane in the air.
steps: Cut a strip of paper about 5 centimetres wide and 25 centimetres long.
Hold one short end just under your bottom lip so the strip hangs down in front of you.
Blow hard and steadily across the top of the paper. Watch the strip rise.
The fast-moving air over the top has lower pressure, so the still air underneath pushes the paper up. Try blowing softer and harder. What changes?
pages.cap: Fast air over the top and slower air underneath lift the paper, just like a wing.

p: A computer is a machine that counts with switches. Each switch is either off or on, which we write as 0 or 1. One switch is called a bit. Put 8 bits in a row and you have a byte, which can stand for 256 different things: a number, a letter or one dot of colour. Everything on a screen, every song and every photo, is just a huge pile of 0s and 1s.

The idea came before the machine. In the 1830s an English mathematician named Charles Babbage designed a steam-powered calculating engine. His friend Ada Lovelace wrote instructions for it in 1843, the first computer program ever written. Babbage never finished building the machine. It would have been the size of a locomotive.
pages.cap: Eight switches, each on or off, make one byte. A byte can hold any number from 0 to 255.
pages.fact: Did you know? A single photo on a phone is about 3 million bytes, or 24 million tiny on-off switches.

pages.h: From a room to your pocket
p: The first general-purpose electronic computer, ENIAC, was switched on in the United States in 1945. It weighed 27 tonnes, filled a room the size of a tennis court and used 18,000 glass tubes that kept burning out. It could do 5,000 additions a second.

In 1947 three scientists invented the transistor, a switch the size of a fingernail with no glass to break. In 1958 engineers learned to carve many transistors onto one chip of silicon, and they kept making them smaller. The chip in a phone today holds about 20 billion transistors and does trillions of operations a second, millions of times more than ENIAC. Put a computer in a machine with motors and you have a robot. About 4 million robots now work in factories.
pages.cap: A robot is a computer with arms, wheels or legs. Its chip is millions of times faster than the first room-sized computers.

pages.q: How much did ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer, weigh?
pages.why: ENIAC weighed 27 tonnes and filled a whole room. The chip in a modern phone weighs less than a gram and is millions of times faster.

p: On 29 October 1969, a student in California tried to send the word LOGIN from one computer to another 560 kilometres away. The system crashed after two letters. Still, L and O had arrived. That was the first message on the network that grew into the internet.

The internet works like the post. A message is cut into small packets, each in its own envelope with an address. The packets travel by any route they can find, through cables under streets and oceans, and get put back together at the other end. If one road is blocked, they take another. In 1983 all the connected networks agreed on one set of rules, and the internet as we know it was born. Today about 5.5 billion people use it.
pages.cap: Most internet traffic travels through cables under the sea, with satellites filling in the gaps.
pages.fact: Did you know? A message from Canada to Australia and back takes about a quarter of a second, most of it inside glass fibres.

p: The internet moves data. The Web is what made it easy to use. In 1989 a British scientist named Tim Berners-Lee worked at a physics laboratory in Switzerland where thousands of researchers could not find each other's documents. He proposed a simple fix: pages of text with links you could click to jump to other pages, anywhere in the world. He built the first website in 1990.

Then he did something rare. In 1993 his laboratory gave the idea away free to everyone, forever. Anyone could build a browser or a website without paying. That is why the Web exploded. There were about 130 websites in 1993. Today there are more than a billion, and about 200 million of them are active.
pages.cap: A link is a bridge between pages. Click it and you cross to a computer that might be on the other side of the planet.
pages.fact: Did you know? The first website is still online. It explains what the Web is and how to make a page.

p: Not every invention was planned. In 1928 a Scottish scientist named Alexander Fleming came back from holiday and found a dish of bacteria ruined by mould. Around the mould, the bacteria were dead. That mould became penicillin, the first antibiotic, and it has saved hundreds of millions of lives.

In 1945 an engineer named Percy Spencer stood near a radar tube and noticed the chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. He put popcorn in front of the tube, and it popped. He had invented the microwave oven. In 1941 a Swiss engineer pulled burrs off his dog and looked at their tiny hooks under a microscope. That became hook-and-loop fasteners. The secret in each case was the same. Lots of people saw. Only one person wondered why.
pages.cap: Fleming's mould killed the bacteria around it. He asked why, and the answer became the first antibiotic.

p: Inventors come in every size. In 1873, a 15-year-old in Maine named Chester Greenwood got cold ears while skating and bent some wire into the first earmuffs. In 1905 an 11-year-old in California, Frank Epperson, left a cup of flavoured soda with a stirring stick outside overnight. It froze. He had made the first ice pop.

Canada has a long list. Insulin, which keeps millions of people with diabetes alive, was discovered in Toronto in 1921. The Robertson square-headed screw came in 1908, the paint roller in 1940, the walkie-talkie in 1937 and the snowmobile in 1937. Every one started with a person who noticed a problem and refused to accept it. Look around you. What is annoying, slow or impossible today? That is where the next invention is hiding.
pages.cap: Some of the most useful inventions came from children who were simply cold, bored or curious.
pages.fact: Did you know? Basketball was invented in 1891 by a Canadian teacher, James Naismith, who nailed two peach baskets to a gym balcony.

items: a new thing or way of doing something that nobody had made before
the rod through the middle of a wheel that lets it spin
the thin thread inside a bulb that glows when electricity heats it
a plug that slides back and forth inside a cylinder, pushed by steam or gas
separate metal letters that can be arranged, inked, printed and reused
the upward push on a wing that keeps an aircraft in the air
the smallest piece of computer information, a 0 or a 1
a tiny electric switch; billions of them make up a computer chip
a small chunk of a message sent across the internet with its own address
an official record that gives an inventor the right to their idea for a set number of years

qs: Which invention in this book would you miss most if it disappeared tomorrow, and how would your day change?
Tim Berners-Lee gave the Web away for free instead of selling it. Was that a good decision? What might have happened if he had charged for it?
Some inventions, like cars and plastics, solved one problem and created new ones. Can you think of an invention we need today to fix a problem an older invention caused?
